**Grenoble** ([/ɡ r ə ˈ n oʊ b əl/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_grə-NOH-bəl_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key");[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-4)French:[[ɡʁənɔbl]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/French "Help:IPA/French")[](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/1/16/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Ltrlg-Grenoble.wav/LL-Q150_%28fra%29-Ltrlg-Grenoble.wav.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:LL-Q150_(fra)-Ltrlg-Grenoble.wav "File:LL-Q150 (fra)-Ltrlg-Grenoble.wav"))[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-5) is the [prefecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefectures_in_France "Prefectures in France") and [largest city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_communes_in_France_with_over_20,000_inhabitants "List of communes in France with over 20,000 inhabitants") of the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère")[department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_France "Departments of France") in the [Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auvergne-Rh%C3%B4ne-Alpes "Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes")[region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regions_of_France "Regions of France") of southeastern France.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-6) It was the capital of the [Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9 "Dauphiné")[historical province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_France "Provinces of France") and lies where the river [Drac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drac_(river) "Drac (river)") flows into the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)") at the foot of the [French Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Alps "French Alps").

The population of the [commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communes_of_France "Communes of France") of Grenoble was 156,140 as of 2023, while the population of the [Grenoble metropolitan area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_metropolitan_area "Grenoble metropolitan area") (French: _[aire d'attraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Functional\_area\_(France) "Functional area (France)") de Grenoble_) was 727,380 in 2023, which makes it the largest metropolis in the Alps, ahead of [Innsbruck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innsbruck "Innsbruck") and [Bolzano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bolzano "Bolzano").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-compar-3) A significant European scientific centre,[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-Graff-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-Pentland-8) the city advertises itself as the "Capital of the Alps", due to its size and its proximity to the mountains. The many suburban communes that make up the rest of the metropolitan area include four with populations exceeding 20,000: [Saint-Martin-d'Hères](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Martin-d'H%C3%A8res "Saint-Martin-d'Hères"), [Échirolles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89chirolles "Échirolles"), [Fontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontaine,_Is%C3%A8re "Fontaine, Isère") and [Voiron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voiron "Voiron").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-pop2017-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-10)

Grenoble's history goes back over 2,000 years, to a time when it was a village of the [Allobroges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allobroges "Allobroges")[Gallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul "Gaul") tribe. It became the capital of the [Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9 "Dauphiné") in the 11th century.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-EB1911-11) This status, consolidated by the annexation to [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France "France"), allowed it to develop its economy. Grenoble then became a parliamentary and military city, close to the border with [Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy "Savoy"), which at the time was part of the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"). Industrial development increased the prominence of Grenoble through several periods of economic expansion over the last three centuries. This started with a booming [glove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glove "Glove") industry in the 18th and 19th centuries, continued with the development of a strong [hydropower](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydropower "Hydropower") industry in the late 19th to early 20th centuries, and ended with a post-[World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II") economic boom symbolized by the holding of the [X Olympic Winter Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Winter_Olympics "1968 Winter Olympics") in 1968.

The city has grown to be one of Europe's most important research, technology and innovation centres, with one in five inhabitants working directly in these fields.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-Graff-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-Pentland-8)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-12) Grenoble was classified as a [global city](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_city "Global city") with the ranking of "sufficiency" by the [Globalization and World Cities Research Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Globalization_and_World_Cities_Research_Network "Globalization and World Cities Research Network") until 2024.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-14) The city held the title of European Green Capital in 2022.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-15)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

For a chronological guide, see [Timeline of Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timeline_of_Grenoble "Timeline of Grenoble").

### Antiquity

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Antiquity")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Vestiges_enceinte_Cularo.JPG/250px-Vestiges_enceinte_Cularo.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vestiges_enceinte_Cularo.JPG)

Remnants of the 3rd century AD Roman walls

The first references to what is now Grenoble date back to 43 BC. [Cularo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cularo "Cularo") was at that time a village of the [Allobroges](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Allobroges "Allobroges")[Gallic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallia "Gallia") tribe, near a bridge across the Isère. Three centuries later and with insecurity rising in the late [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"), a strong [wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defensive_wall "Defensive wall") was built around the small town in 286 AD.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-16)

The [Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Roman_Empire "Western Roman Empire")[Gratian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gratian "Gratian") visited Cularo and, touched by the people's welcome, made the village a Roman city.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-17) In honour of this, Cularo was renamed **Gratianopolis** ("city of Gratian") in 381. Through regular historical sound shifts, this later became _Graignovol_[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-18) during the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), and this then became _Grenoble_.

Christianity spread to the region during the 4th century, and the [diocese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Diocese_of_Grenoble-Vienne "Roman Catholic Diocese of Grenoble-Vienne") of Grenoble was founded in 377 AD. From that time on, the bishops exercised significant political power over the city. Until the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"), they styled themselves the "bishops and princes of Grenoble".[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-19)

### Middle Ages

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Middle Ages")]

After the collapse of the [Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire"), the city became part of the first [Burgundian kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Burgundy "Kingdom of Burgundy") in the 5th century and of the later [Kingdom of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Burgundy-Arles "Kingdom of Burgundy-Arles") until 1032, when it was integrated into the [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire"). The Burgundian rule was interrupted between 942 and 970 by Arab rule based in [Fraxinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraxinet "Fraxinet").

Grenoble grew significantly in the 11th century when the [Counts of Albon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Counts_of_Albon_and_Dauphins_of_Viennois "List of Counts of Albon and Dauphins of Viennois") chose the city as the capital of their territories. Their possessions at the time were a patchwork of several territories sprawled across the region,[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-20) and the central position of Grenoble allowed the Counts to strengthen their authority. When they later adopted the title of "[Dauphins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin_of_France "Dauphin of France")", Grenoble became the capital of the State of [Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9 "Dauphiné").

Despite their status, the Counts had to share authority over the city with the Bishop of Grenoble. One of the most famous of those was [Saint Hugh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_of_Ch%C3%A2teauneuf "Hugh of Châteauneuf"). Under his rule, the city's bridge was rebuilt, and a regular and [leper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leper "Leper") hospital was built.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-21)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5a/Arms_of_the_Dauphin_of_France.svg/120px-Arms_of_the_Dauphin_of_France.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Arms_of_the_Dauphin_of_France.svg)

Coat of arms of the Dauphiné after becoming a province of France

The inhabitants of Grenoble took advantage of the conflicts between the Counts and the bishops and obtained the recognition of a Charter of Customs that guaranteed their rights.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-22) That charter was confirmed by Kings [Louis XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI "Louis XI") in 1447 and [Francis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France") in 1541.

In 1336, the last Dauphin [Humbert II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humbert_II_of_Viennois "Humbert II of Viennois") founded a court of justice, the [Conseil delphinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil_delphinal?action=edit&redlink=1 "Conseil delphinal (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conseil%20delphinal "fr:Conseil delphinal")], which settled at Grenoble in 1340. He also established the [University of Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Grenoble "University of Grenoble") in 1339. Without an heir and deep into debt, Humbert sold his state to France in 1349, on the condition that the heir to the [French crown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_French_monarchs "List of French monarchs") used the title of _[Dauphin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin\_of\_France "Dauphin of France")_. The first one, the future [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V_of_France "Charles V of France"), spent nine months in Grenoble. The city remained the capital of the Dauphiné,[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-EB1911-11) henceforth a [province of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_France "Provinces of France"), and the [Estates of Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_Provincial_(France) "States Provincial (France)") were created.

The only Dauphin who governed his province was the future [Louis XI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XI "Louis XI"), whose "reign" lasted from 1447 to 1456. It was only under his rule that Dauphiné properly joined the Kingdom of France. The Old Conseil Delphinal became a [Parlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement "Parlement") (the third in France after the Parliaments of Paris and Toulouse), strengthening the status of Grenoble as a Provincial capital. He also ordered the construction of the Palais du Parlement (finished under [Francis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France")) and ensured that the Bishop pledged allegiance, thus unifying the political control of the city.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-23)

At that time, Grenoble was a crossroads between [Vienne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienne,_Is%C3%A8re "Vienne, Isère"), Geneva, Italy, and [Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy "Savoy"). It was the industrial centre of the Dauphiné and the province's biggest city, but a rather small one.

### Renaissance

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Renaissance")]

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/82/Francois-de-bonne-duc-de-le.jpg/250px-Francois-de-bonne-duc-de-le.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Francois-de-bonne-duc-de-le.jpg)

François de Bonne, duc de Lesdiguières

Owing to Grenoble's geographical situation, French troops were garrisoned in the city and its region during the [Italian Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Wars "Italian Wars"). [Charles VIII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_VIII_of_France "Charles VIII of France"), [Louis XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XII "Louis XII"), and [Francis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_I_of_France "Francis I of France") went several times to Grenoble. Its people consequently had to suffer from the exactions of the soldiers.

The nobility of the region took part in various battles ([Marignano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marignano "Battle of Marignano"), [Pavia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Pavia "Battle of Pavia")) and in doing so gained significant prestige.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-24) The best-known of its members was [Bayard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Terrail,_seigneur_de_Bayard "Pierre Terrail, seigneur de Bayard"), "the knight without fear and beyond reproach".

Grenoble suffered as a result of the [French Wars of Religion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Wars_of_Religion "French Wars of Religion"). The Dauphiné was indeed an important settlement for Protestants and therefore experienced several conflicts. The [baron des Adrets](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Beaumont,_baron_des_Adrets "François de Beaumont, baron des Adrets"), the leader of the [Huguenots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huguenots "Huguenots"), pillaged the [Cathedral of Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Cathedral "Grenoble Cathedral") and destroyed the tombs of the former Dauphins.

In August 1575, [Lesdiguières](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Bonne,_duc_de_Lesdigui%C3%A8res "François de Bonne, duc de Lesdiguières") became the new leader of the Protestants and, thanks to the accession of [Henry IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_IV_of_France "Henry IV of France") to the throne of France, allied himself with the governor and the lieutenant general of the Dauphiné. But this alliance did not bring an end to the conflicts. Indeed, a Catholic movement, the _Ligue_, which took Grenoble in December 1590, refused to make peace. After months of assaults, Lesdiguières defeated the Ligue and took back Grenoble. He became the leader of the entire province.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-25)

Lesdiguières became the lieutenant-general of the Dauphiné and administered the Province from 1591 to 1626. He began the construction of the [Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille_(Grenoble) "Bastille (Grenoble)") to protect the city and ordered the construction of new walls, increasing the city's size. He also constructed the Hôtel Lesdiguières, built new fountains, and dug sewers.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-26)

In 1689, the bishop [Étienne Le Camus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89tienne_Le_Camus "Étienne Le Camus") launched the construction of [Saint-Louis Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Louis_Church,_Grenoble "Saint-Louis Church, Grenoble").

### From Louis XIV to the French Revolution

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: From Louis XIV to the French Revolution")]

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Grenoble_serr%C3%A9_-_plan-relief_1848.jpg/250px-Grenoble_serr%C3%A9_-_plan-relief_1848.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Grenoble_serr%C3%A9_-_plan-relief_1848.jpg)

Grenoble [plan-relief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plan-relief "Plan-relief") (1848)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Journ%C3%A9e_des_Tuiles_%28Alexandre_Debelle%29%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_de_la_R%C3%A9volution_fran%C3%A7aise_-_Vizille.jpg/250px-Journ%C3%A9e_des_Tuiles_%28Alexandre_Debelle%29%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_de_la_R%C3%A9volution_fran%C3%A7aise_-_Vizille.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Journ%C3%A9e_des_Tuiles_(Alexandre_Debelle),_Mus%C3%A9e_de_la_R%C3%A9volution_fran%C3%A7aise_-_Vizille.jpg)

_[Day of the Tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day\_of\_the\_Tiles "Day of the Tiles")_, 1890 painting by [Alexandre Debelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Debelle "Alexandre Debelle"),  
 ([Musée de la Révolution française](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_la_R%C3%A9volution_fran%C3%A7aise "Musée de la Révolution française"))

The revocation of the [Edict of Nantes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Nantes "Edict of Nantes") by [Louis XIV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XIV "Louis XIV") caused the departure of 2,000 Protestants from Grenoble, weakening the city's economy.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-27) However, it also weakened the competing glove industry of [Grasse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grasse "Grasse"), leaving the glove factories of Grenoble without any competition.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-Dauphin%C3%A9_1933,_p98-28) This allowed a stronger economic development for the city during the 18th century. At the beginning of that century, only 12 glovers made 180,000 gloves each year; by 1787, 64 glovers made 1,920,000 gloves each year.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-Dauphin%C3%A9_1933,_p98-28)

The city gained some notoriety on 7 June 1788 when the townspeople assaulted troops of [Louis XVI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XVI "Louis XVI") in the "[Day of the Tiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_of_the_Tiles "Day of the Tiles")".[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-EB1911-11) The people attacked the royal troops to prevent an expulsion of the notables of the city, which would have seriously endangered the economic prosperity of Grenoble. Following these events, the [Assembly of Vizille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assembly_of_Vizille "Assembly of Vizille") took place. Its members organized the meeting of the old [Estates General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Estates-General_of_1789 "Estates-General of 1789"), thus beginning the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"). During the Revolution, Grenoble was represented in Paris by two illustrious notables, [Jean Joseph Mounier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Joseph_Mounier "Jean Joseph Mounier") and [Antoine Barnave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Barnave "Antoine Barnave").

In 1790, the Dauphiné was divided into three [departments](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Departments_of_France "Departments of France"), and Grenoble became the _chef-lieu_ of the [Isère department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère"). Only two [refractory priests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Refractory_clergy "Refractory clergy") were executed at Grenoble during the [Reign of Terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reign_of_Terror "Reign of Terror").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-29)[Pope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope "Pope")[Pius VI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pius_VI "Pius VI"), prisoner of France, spent two days at Grenoble in 1799[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-30) before going to [Valence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valence,_Dr%C3%B4me "Valence, Drôme") where he died at 81 six weeks after his arrival.

### 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 19th century")]

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9c/Fortifications_Bastille_-_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Fortifications_Bastille_-_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fortifications_Bastille_-_Grenoble.JPG)

Ramparts close to the Porte Saint Laurent

The establishment of the [Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_French_Empire "First French Empire") was overwhelmingly approved (in Isère, the results showed 82,084 yes and only 12 no).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-31) Grenoble held for the second time a prisoner Pope in 1809, when [Pius VII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pius_VII "Pius VII") spent 10 days in the city en route to his exile in [Fontainebleau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fontainebleau "Fontainebleau").

In 1813, Grenoble was under threat from the Austrian army, which invaded Switzerland and [Savoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savoy "Savoy"). The well-defended city contained the Austrian attacks, and the French army defeated the Austrians, forcing them to withdraw at [Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geneva "Geneva"). However, the later [invasion of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Six_Days_Campaign "Six Days Campaign") in 1814 resulted in the capitulation of the troops and the occupation of the city.

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Retour_de_Napoleon_d%27_Isle_d%27Elbe%2C_by_Charles_de_Steuben.jpg/250px-Retour_de_Napoleon_d%27_Isle_d%27Elbe%2C_by_Charles_de_Steuben.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Retour_de_Napoleon_d'_Isle_d'Elbe,_by_Charles_de_Steuben.jpg)

_[Napoleon's Return from Elba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon's\_Return\_from\_Elba\_(painting) "Napoleon's Return from Elba (painting)")_ by [Charles de Steuben](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Steuben "Charles de Steuben"), 1818

During his [return](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Days "Hundred Days") from the island of [Elba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elba "Elba") in 1815, Napoleon took a [road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Route_Napoleon "Route Napoleon") that led him near Grenoble at [Laffrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laffrey "Laffrey"). There he met the Royalist Régiment d'Angoulême (former 5th) of [Louis XVIII's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_XVIII "Louis XVIII")[Royal Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Royal_Army "French Royal Army"). Napoleon stepped toward the soldiers and said these famous words: "If there is among you a soldier who wants to kill his Emperor, here I am." The soldiers all joined his cause. After that, Napoleon was acclaimed at Grenoble and General [Jean Gabriel Marchand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Gabriel_Marchand "Jean Gabriel Marchand") could not prevent Napoleon from entering the city through the Bonne gate. He said later: "From [Cannes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cannes "Cannes") to Grenoble, I still was an adventurer; in that last city, I came back a sovereign".[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-32) But after the defeat of [Waterloo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Waterloo "Battle of Waterloo"), the region suffered from a new invasion of Austrian and Sardinian troops.

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d9/Fontaine_trois_ordres_-_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Fontaine_trois_ordres_-_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fontaine_trois_ordres_-_Grenoble.JPG)

Fountain of the Three Orders (1897)

The 19th century saw significant industrial development of Grenoble. The glove factories reached their Golden Age, and their products were exported to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), and [Russia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Russia "Russia").[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-33)

[General Haxo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Nicolas_Beno%C3%AEt,_Baron_Haxo "François Nicolas Benoît, Baron Haxo") transformed the [Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille_(Grenoble) "Bastille (Grenoble)") fortress, which took on its present aspect between 1824 and 1848. The [Second Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_French_Empire "Second French Empire") saw the construction of the French railway network, and the first trains arrived at Grenoble in 1858. Shortly thereafter Grenoble experienced widespread destruction by [extensive flooding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Flood_1859 "Grenoble Flood 1859") in 1859.

In 1869, engineer [Aristide Bergès](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristide_Berg%C3%A8s?action=edit&redlink=1 "Aristide Bergès (page does not exist)") played a major role in industrializing hydroelectricity production. With the development of his paper mills, he accelerated the economic development of the Grésivaudan valley and Grenoble.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

On 4 August 1897, a stone and bronze fountain was inaugurated in Grenoble to commemorate the pre-revolutionary events of June 1788. Built by the sculptor [Henri Ding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Ding "Henri Ding"), the Fountain of the Three Orders, which represents three characters, is located on Place Notre-Dame. People in Grenoble interpret these characters as follows: "Is it raining?" inquires the [third estate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_third_estate "The third estate"); "Please heaven it had rained", lament the [clergy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clergy "Clergy"); and "It will rain", proclaims the [nobility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobility "Nobility").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-34)

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 20th century")]

[World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") accelerated Grenoble's economic development.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-35) To sustain the war effort, new hydroelectric industries developed along the various rivers of the region, and several existing companies moved into the armaments industry (for example in [Livet-et-Gavet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livet-et-Gavet "Livet-et-Gavet")). Electrochemical factories were also established in the area surrounding Grenoble, initially to produce chemical weapons. This development resulted in significant immigration to Grenoble, particularly from Italian workers who settled in the Saint-Laurent neighborhood.

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a1/Entr%C3%A9e_exposition_H.B._-_Grenoble.jpg/250px-Entr%C3%A9e_exposition_H.B._-_Grenoble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Entr%C3%A9e_exposition_H.B._-_Grenoble.jpg)

Gate of the exposition in 1925

The economic development of the city was highlighted by the organization of the [International Exhibition of Hydropower and Tourism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Exhibition_of_Hydropower_and_Tourism "International Exhibition of Hydropower and Tourism") in 1925, which was visited by more than 1 million people.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-36)[_[circular reference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Wikipedia\_and\_sources\_that\_mirror\_or\_use\_it "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] The organization of this exhibition forced the military to remove the old city walls and allowed the expansion of the city to the south. This exhibition also highlighted the city's hydropower industry and the region's tourist attractions.

The site of the exhibition became an urban park in 1926, named [Parc Paul Mistral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parc_Paul_Mistral "Parc Paul Mistral") after the death of the mayor in 1932. The only building of this exhibition remaining in the park is the crumbling [Tour Perret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perret_tower_(Grenoble) "Perret tower (Grenoble)"), which has been closed to the public since 1960 due to its very poor state of maintenance.

#### World War II

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: World War II")]

During World War II, at the [Battle of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_France "Battle of France"), the German invasion was stopped near Grenoble at [Voreppe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voreppe "Voreppe") by the forces of [General Cartier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/General_Cartier?action=edit&redlink=1 "General Cartier (page does not exist)"). The French forces resisted until the armistice, after which Grenoble was part of the [French State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_State "French State") before an Italian occupation from 1942 to 1943. The relative tolerance of the Italian occupiers towards the Jewish populations resulted in a significant number moving to the region from the German-occupied parts of France.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-37)

Grenoble was extremely active in the [Résistance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Resistance "French Resistance") against the occupation. Its action was symbolized by figures such as [Eugène Chavant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Chavant "Eugène Chavant"), Léon Martin, and [Marie Reynoard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie_Reynoard "Marie Reynoard").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-ordredelaliberation.fr-38) The University of Grenoble supported the clandestine operations and provided false documentation for young people to prevent them from being assigned to [STO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Service_du_Travail_Obligatoire "Service du Travail Obligatoire").

In September 1943, German troops occupied Grenoble, escalating the conflict with the clandestine movements. On 11 November 1943 (the anniversary of the [armistice of 1918](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I")), massive strikes and demonstrations took place in front of the local collaboration offices. In response, the occupiers arrested 400 demonstrators in the streets. On 13 November, the resistance blew up the artillery at the Polygon, which was a psychological shock for an enemy who then intensified the repression. On 25 November, the occupiers killed 11 members of the Résistance organizations of Grenoble. This violent crackdown was nicknamed "[Grenoble's Saint-Bartholomew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble's_Saint-Bartholomew "Grenoble's Saint-Bartholomew")".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-39) From these events, Grenoble was styled by the [Free French Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_French_Forces "Free French Forces") the title of _Capital of the [Maquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maquis\_(World\_War\_II) "Maquis (World War II)")_ on the antennas of the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Broadcasting_Corporation "British Broadcasting Corporation").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-40)

This event only intensified the activities of Grenoble's resistance movements. The Germans could not prevent the destruction of their new arsenal on 2 December at the Bonne Barracks. After the [Normandy landing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Invasion_of_Normandy "Invasion of Normandy"), resistance operations reached their peak, with numerous attacks considerably hampering the activity of German troops. With the [landing in Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operation_Dragoon "Operation Dragoon"), German troops evacuated the city on 22 August 1944. On 5 November 1944, General [Charles de Gaulle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_de_Gaulle "Charles de Gaulle") came to Grenoble and bestowed on the city the _[Compagnon de la Libération](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordre\_de\_la\_Lib%C3%A9ration "Ordre de la Libération")_ to recognise "a heroic city at the peak of the French resistance and combat for the liberation".[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-ordredelaliberation.fr-38)

#### Post-war

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Post-war")]

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/54/H%C3%B4tel_de_ville_de_Grenoble_depuis_La_Bastille.jpg/250px-H%C3%B4tel_de_ville_de_Grenoble_depuis_La_Bastille.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:H%C3%B4tel_de_ville_de_Grenoble_depuis_La_Bastille.jpg)

The [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Grenoble "Hôtel de Ville, Grenoble")

In 1955, future [physics Nobel Prize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physics "Nobel Prize in Physics") laureate [Louis Néel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louis_N%C3%A9el "Louis Néel") created the Grenoble Center for Nuclear Studies (CENG), resulting in the birth of the Grenoble model, a combination of research and industry. The first stone was laid in December 1956.

In 1968, Grenoble hosted the [X Olympic Winter Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Winter_Olympics "1968 Winter Olympics"). This event helped modernize the city with the development of infrastructure such as an airport, motorways, the new [Hôtel de Ville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/H%C3%B4tel_de_Ville,_Grenoble "Hôtel de Ville, Grenoble") (town hall), and a new train station.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-41) It also helped the development of ski resorts like [Chamrousse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chamrousse "Chamrousse"), [Les Deux Alpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Les_Deux_Alpes "Les Deux Alpes"), and [Villard-de-Lans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Villard-de-Lans "Villard-de-Lans").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-42)

### 21st century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: 21st century")]

Since 2017, anarchist movements have been behind a wave of arson attacks in Grenoble. During the last week of August 2023, a police operation was carried out in the Saint-Bruno district of Grenoble, after the city experienced a new series of gangland killings during the summer. Numerous recurring security problems were observed in the immediate vicinity of Place Saint-Bruno and Cours Berriat, particularly related to drug trafficking and arms trafficking.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-43)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Geography")]

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2f/Moucherotte_23_12_11_092_%282%29_final.JPG/250px-Moucherotte_23_12_11_092_%282%29_final.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Moucherotte_23_12_11_092_(2)_final.JPG)

Grenoble with the [Dauphiné Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9_Alps "Dauphiné Alps") in the background

Grenoble is surrounded by mountains. To the north lies the [Chartreuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chartreuse_Mountains "Chartreuse Mountains"), to the south and west the [Vercors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vercors_Plateau "Vercors Plateau"), and to the east the [Belledonne range](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belledonne "Belledonne"). Grenoble is regarded as the capital of the French Alps. It is the centre of the [Grenoble urban unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_urban_unit "Grenoble urban unit") (agglomeration).[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-44)

Except for a few dozen houses on the slopes of the [Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille_(Grenoble) "Bastille (Grenoble)") hill of Chartreuse, Grenoble is exclusively built on the alluvial plain of the rivers [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)") and [Drac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drac_(river) "Drac (river)") at an altitude of 214 metres (702 ft). As a result, the city itself is extremely flat. Mountain sports are an important tourist attraction in summer and winter. Twenty large and small ski resorts surround the city, the nearest being [Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Sappey-en-Chartreuse "Le Sappey-en-Chartreuse"), which is about 15 minutes away by car.

Historically, Grenoble and the surrounding areas were heavy industry and mining sites.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-45) Abandoned mills and factories can be found in small towns and villages, and a few have been converted to tourist attractions, such as the coal mine at [La Mure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Mure "La Mure").

### Climate

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Climate")]

The climate in Grenoble is much gloomier than in the Mediterranean region, although less so than in Northern France. Rainfall is quite heavy by French standards, although the number of rainy days is relatively moderate.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] As a result of winter lows averaging below freezing, snowfall also occurs, although the Grenoble Airport area itself is too mild to sustain a snowpack all winter, unlike the surrounding mountains. The record low of −27.1°C (−16.8°F) decisively indicates the continental influence, being colder than records in typical maritime climates. Winter nights are also colder than in all other French lowland areas.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Different weather stations report significant variation in climate. [Grenoble Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Airport "Grenoble Airport"), located 40 km (25 mi) northwest of the city, has a range from [temperate continental climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Temperate_continental_climate "Temperate continental climate") to [oceanic climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceanic_climate "Oceanic climate") ([Köppen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/K%C3%B6ppen_climate_classification "Köppen climate classification"): Cfb, [Trewartha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trewartha_climate_classification "Trewartha climate classification"): Dc, Do) depending on the chosen classifications. The area contains significant seasonal differences between warm to hot summers and cool to cold winters. Both temperatures above 30°C (86°F) for the summer months and winter [air frosts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Air_frost "Air frost") are common.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The Grenoble metropolitan area experiences two different microclimates: one more windy and cold to the west, the other, on the contrary, not very windy and warmer to the east.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] However, the city of Grenoble features a [humid subtropical climate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humid_subtropical_climate "Humid subtropical climate") (Köppen: Cfa) with no dry season. Although the record is incomplete, the newer station will meet the humid subtropical classification if maintained for the required 30-year period.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## Urbanism and architecture

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Urbanism and architecture")]

The Bouchayer-Viallet site is a powerful symbol of Grenoble's industrial past.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-51) This former factory is now converted into a dual-purpose area more closely linked to the Berriat neighbourhood. Innovative business activities as [Apple Inc.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apple_Inc. "Apple Inc.")[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-52) co-exist with housing, sporting facilities, contemporary music venue and arts centres as [Le Magasin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Magasin "Le Magasin"). At the entrance to the Bouchayer-Viallet site, Square des Fusillés has been redeveloped and extended taking over an old car park, to facilitate access from the tramway stop and Cours Berriat.

Redevelopment of the former De Bonne barracks was an important step in the drive to launch [sustainable housing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_building "Green building") in France. In 2009, the site of De Bonne was distinguished as the best eco-neighborhood in France.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-53) A shopping mall contains 53 shops arranged around an inner concourse, with one side opening onto the park and the other connecting to the town.

### La Bastille

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: La Bastille")]

The [Bastille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bastille_(Grenoble) "Bastille (Grenoble)"), an ancient series of fortifications on the mountainside, overlooks Grenoble on the northern side and is visible from many points in the city. The Bastille is one of Grenoble's most visited tourist attractions and provides a good vantage point over both the town below and the surrounding mountains.

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Seilbahn-Grenoble.JPG/250px-Seilbahn-Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Seilbahn-Grenoble.JPG)

"Les Bulles": the cable cars

The Bastille fort was begun in the [Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Ages "Middle Ages"), and later centuries saw extensive additions, including a semi-underground defense network. The Bastille has been credited as the most extensive example of early 18th-century fortifications in all of France. It then held an important strategic point on the French [Alpine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps") frontier with the [Kingdom of Sardinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Sardinia_(1720%E2%80%931861) "Kingdom of Sardinia (1720–1861)").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-54)

The first cable transport system, installed on the Bastille in 1875, was built by the Porte de France Cement Company for freight. This cable transport system connected a quarry on Mount Jalla, just over the Bastille, and Grenoble. It was abandoned in the early 20th century.

Since 1934, the Bastille has been the destination of the "[Grenoble-Bastille cable car](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble-Bastille_cable_car "Grenoble-Bastille cable car")". This system of mostly transparent egg-shaped [cable cars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aerial_tramway "Aerial tramway") known to locals as "Les Bulles" (the bubbles) provides the occupants with an excellent view over the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)"). At the top are two restaurants and installed in the casemates of the fort itself since June 2006, the Bastille Art Centre allows visitors to see contemporary art exhibitions. There is also a small military museum on mountain troops (_Musée des troupes de montagne_) and, since 2000, a memorial to the mountain troops (_Mémorial national des troupes de montagne_) further along the road, on top of the hill.

### Palace of the Parliament of Dauphiné

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Palace of the Parliament of Dauphiné")]

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/88/Parlement_du_Dauphin%C3%A9_-_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Parlement_du_Dauphin%C3%A9_-_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Parlement_du_Dauphin%C3%A9_-_Grenoble.JPG)

Palace of the [Parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament "Parliament") of [Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9 "Dauphiné")

This renaissance palace was constructed at the Place Saint André around 1500 and extended in 1539. It was the location of the [Parlement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parlement "Parlement") of [Dauphiné](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dauphin%C3%A9 "Dauphiné") until the [French Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Revolution "French Revolution"). It then became the Grenoble courthouse, until the courts were moved to a modern building in 2002. The left wing of the palace was extended in 1897. The front of the former seat of the nearby Dauphiné Parlement combines elements from a gothic chapel and a Renaissance façade.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-55)

The building now belongs to the Isère Council (Conseil Général de l'Isère). An ongoing renovation project will give this building a new life whilst preserving its patrimonial character and adding a modern touch.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-56)

### Museum of Grenoble

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Museum of Grenoble")]

The city's most prized museum, the [Museum of Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Grenoble "Museum of Grenoble") (_Musée de Grenoble_), welcomes 200,000 visitors a year. It is primarily renowned for its extensive paintings collection, which covers Western paintings from the Middle Ages to the 21st century. In the early 20th century, the Museum of Grenoble became the first French museum to open its collections to modern art, and its collection of modern and contemporary art has grown to become one of the largest in Europe. The painting holdings include works by painters such as [Veronese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paolo_Veronese "Paolo Veronese"), [Rubens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubens "Rubens"), [Zurbarán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zurbar%C3%A1n "Zurbarán"), [Ingres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingres "Ingres"), [Delacroix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Delacroix "Eugène Delacroix"), [Renoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre-Auguste_Renoir "Pierre-Auguste Renoir"), [Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), [Signac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac "Paul Signac"), [Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Monet "Claude Monet"), [Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse"), [Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picasso "Picasso"), [Kandinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassily_Kandinsky "Wassily Kandinsky"), [Joan Miró](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Mir%C3%B3 "Joan Miró"), [Paul Klee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Klee "Paul Klee"), [Giorgio de Chirico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_de_Chirico "Giorgio de Chirico") and [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"). The museum also presents a few Egyptian antiquities as well as Greek and Roman artifacts. The Sculpture collection features works by [Auguste Rodin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Rodin "Auguste Rodin"), [Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matisse "Matisse"), [Alberto Giacometti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Giacometti "Alberto Giacometti") and [Alexander Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder"). In April 2010, the _prophetess of Antinoe_, a 6th-century mummy discovered in 1907 in the [Coptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copts "Copts")[necropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necropolis "Necropolis") of [Antinoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antinopolis "Antinopolis") in Middle Egypt, returned to the Museum of Grenoble, after more than fifty years of absence and extensive restoration.

### Archaeological museums

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Archaeological museums")]

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e7/Mus%C3%A9e_arch%C3%A9ologique_de_Grenoble_027.jpg/250px-Mus%C3%A9e_arch%C3%A9ologique_de_Grenoble_027.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mus%C3%A9e_arch%C3%A9ologique_de_Grenoble_027.jpg)

[Archaeological](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Archaeological_Museum "Grenoble Archaeological Museum") museum with the vestiges protected by a new cover of glass and metal (Place Saint-Laurent)

Situated on the right bank of the Isère, on Place Saint-Laurent, the [Grenoble Archaeological Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Archaeological_Museum "Grenoble Archaeological Museum") presents the archaeological excavations done on its location. The vestiges date back to the 3rd century AD and provide a timeline of the history of Christianity in the region. The museum is situated below a 12th-century Benedictine church, under which [Jacques Joseph Champollion-Figeac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Joseph_Champollion-Figeac "Jacques Joseph Champollion-Figeac"), brother of famed egyptologist [Jean-François Champollion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_Champollion "Jean-François Champollion"), discovered a 6th-century AD church in 1803. It was one of the first classified monuments in France thanks to the intervention of [Prosper Mérimée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prosper_M%C3%A9rim%C3%A9e "Prosper Mérimée"), historic monument inspector.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-57) Systematic excavations were conducted from 1978 to 2011, as part of a regional research program on the evolution of churches during the Middle Ages. After eight years of work, the museum reopened on 6 May 2011.

The [Musée de l'Ancien Évêché](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9 "Musée de l'Ancien Évêché") is the second archaeological museum in the city and is located near the [Grenoble Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Cathedral "Grenoble Cathedral"). Installed in 1998, it houses the first baptistery of the city.

The Grenoble town hall hosts a bust of Stendhal by sculptor [Pierre Charles Lenoir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Charles_Lenoir "Pierre Charles Lenoir").

## Education and science

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: Education and science")]

### Secondary level

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Secondary level")]

The large community of both foreign students and foreign researchers prompted the creation of an international school. The [Cité Scolaire Internationale Europole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cit%C3%A9_Scolaire_Internationale_de_Grenoble "Cité Scolaire Internationale de Grenoble") (CSI Europole) was formerly housed within the _[Lycée Stendhal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e\_Stendhal "Lycée Stendhal")_ across from the _[Maison du Tourisme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maison\_du\_Tourisme "Maison du Tourisme")_, but later moved to its own building in the [Europole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europole?action=edit&redlink=1 "Europole (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Europole "fr:Europole")] district. In the centre of the city, two high schools have provided education to the isérois for more than three centuries. The oldest one, the [Lycée Stendhal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Stendhal "Lycée Stendhal"), was founded in 1651[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-58) as a Jesuit College. An astronomical and astrological sundial created in the college's main building in 1673 can still be visited today. The second-oldest higher education establishment in Grenoble is the [Lycée Champollion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Champollion "Lycée Champollion"), completed in 1887 to offer an excellent education to both high school students and students of preparatory classes.

### Higher education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Higher education")]

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Domaine_universitaire_Grenoble.jpg/250px-Domaine_universitaire_Grenoble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Domaine_universitaire_Grenoble.jpg)

Campus of the [Université Grenoble Alpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_Grenoble_Alpes "Université Grenoble Alpes")

The city is an important university centre with over 54,000 students in 2013, of whom 16% arrive from abroad.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-59)

In a 1339 [papal bull](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papal_bull "Papal bull"), Pope [Benedict XII](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benedict_XII "Benedict XII") commissioned the establishment of the [University of Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_Grenoble_Alpes "Université Grenoble Alpes").

In 1965, the university mostly relocated from downtown to a suburban main campus outside of the city in [Saint Martin d'Hères](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint-Martin-d'H%C3%A8res "Saint-Martin-d'Hères") (with some parts in [Gières](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gi%C3%A8res "Gières")). However, smaller campuses remain both downtown and in the northwestern part of the city known as the _[Polygone Scientifique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygone\_Scientifique "Polygone Scientifique")_ ("Scientific Polygon").

From 1970 to 2015, the university was divided into four separate institutions sharing the campus grounds, some buildings and laboratories, and even part of their administration:

*   Grenoble I – [Joseph Fourier University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Fourier_University "Joseph Fourier University") (sciences, health, technologies)
*   Grenoble II – [Pierre Mendès-France University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Mend%C3%A8s-France_University "Pierre Mendès-France University") (social sciences) 
    *   which includes the [Institute of political studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_d'%C3%A9tudes_politiques_de_Grenoble "Institut d'études politiques de Grenoble")

*   Grenoble III – [Stendhal University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stendhal_University "Stendhal University") (humanities)
*   [Grenoble Institute of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Institute_of_Technology "Grenoble Institute of Technology") (INPG or Grenoble-INP) is a federation of engineering colleges.

The first three of those merged back on 1 January 2016 to form the [Université Grenoble Alpes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universit%C3%A9_Grenoble_Alpes "Université Grenoble Alpes"), and the last one joined them on 1 January 2020.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-60)

Grenoble Campus of the [ENAC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89cole_nationale_de_l'aviation_civile "École nationale de l'aviation civile")

Campuses are also located in Grenoble for:

*   École d'Architecture de Grenoble (School of Architecture of Grenoble) and
*   [Grenoble École de Management](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_%C3%89cole_de_Management "Grenoble École de Management") (Grenoble School of Management) triple accredited [AMBA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_of_MBAs "Association of MBAs")-[EQUIS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/EFMD_Quality_Improvement_System "EFMD Quality Improvement System")-[AACSB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_to_Advance_Collegiate_Schools_of_Business "Association to Advance Collegiate Schools of Business") Business School.

#### Science and engineering

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Grenoble&action=edit&section=25 "Edit section: Science and engineering")]

[![Image 32](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/94/Esrf_grenoble.jpg/250px-Esrf_grenoble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Esrf_grenoble.jpg)

Site of [European Synchrotron Radiation Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Synchrotron_Radiation_Facility "European Synchrotron Radiation Facility"), [Institut Laue-Langevin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_Laue-Langevin "Institut Laue-Langevin") and [European Molecular Biology Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Molecular_Biology_Laboratory "European Molecular Biology Laboratory") at the western end of the _[Polygone Scientifique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygone\_Scientifique "Polygone Scientifique")_

Grenoble is a major scientific centre, especially in the fields of [physics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physics "Physics"), [computer science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_science "Computer science"), and [applied mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Applied_mathematics "Applied mathematics"): [Universite Joseph Fourier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Fourier_University "Joseph Fourier University") (UJF) is one of the leading French scientific universities while the Grenoble Institute of Technology trains more than 5,000 engineers every year in key technology disciplines. Grenoble's high-tech expertise is organized mainly around three domains: information technology, biotechnologies, and new technologies of energy.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-61)

Many fundamental and applied scientific research laboratories are conjointly managed by Joseph Fourier University, Grenoble Institute of Technology, and the French _[National Centre for Scientific Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French\_National\_Centre\_for\_Scientific\_Research "French National Centre for Scientific Research")_ (CNRS). Numerous other scientific laboratories are managed independently or in collaboration with the CNRS and the French _[National Institute for Research in Computer Science and Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut\_national\_de\_recherche\_en\_informatique\_et\_en\_automatique "Institut national de recherche en informatique et en automatique")_ (INRIA).

Other research centres in or near Grenoble include the [European Synchrotron Radiation Facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Synchrotron_Radiation_Facility "European Synchrotron Radiation Facility") (ESRF), the [Institut Laue-Langevin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_Laue-Langevin "Institut Laue-Langevin") (ILL), the [European Molecular Biology Laboratory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Molecular_Biology_Laboratory "European Molecular Biology Laboratory") (EMBL), the [Institut de radioastronomie millimétrique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_de_radioastronomie_millim%C3%A9trique "Institut de radioastronomie millimétrique"), one of the main research facilities of the [Commissariat à l'Énergie Atomique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commissariat_%C3%A0_l'%C3%A9nergie_atomique "Commissariat à l'énergie atomique") (Nuclear Energy Commission, CEA), the [LNCMI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LNCMI "LNCMI") and the European branch of [Xerox Research](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xerox "Xerox") (whose most notable center was [PARC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/PARC_(company) "PARC (company)")). [Leti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CEA-Leti:_Laboratoire_d'%C3%A9lectronique_des_technologies_de_l'information "CEA-Leti: Laboratoire d'électronique des technologies de l'information") and the recent development of [Minatec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minatec "Minatec"), a centre for innovation in micro- and nano-technology, only increases Grenoble's position as a European scientific centre.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-62) Biotechnologies are also well represented in the Grenoble region with the molecular biology research center [BioMérieux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BioM%C3%A9rieux "BioMérieux"), the [Clinatec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clinatec "Clinatec") center, the regional center NanoBio and many ramifications of the global competitiveness cluster Lyonbiopôle.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-63)

Meanwhile, Grenoble has large laboratories related to space and to the understanding and observation of the universe as the [Institut de radioastronomie millimétrique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_de_radioastronomie_millim%C3%A9trique "Institut de radioastronomie millimétrique"), the [Institut de planétologie et d'astrophysique de Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_de_plan%C3%A9tologie_et_d'astrophysique_de_Grenoble?action=edit&redlink=1 "Institut de planétologie et d'astrophysique de Grenoble (page does not exist)"),[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-64) the [Laboratoire de physique subatomique et de cosmologie de Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laboratoire_de_physique_subatomique_et_de_cosmologie_de_Grenoble?action=edit&redlink=1 "Laboratoire de physique subatomique et de cosmologie de Grenoble (page does not exist)"), the [Institut Néel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_N%C3%A9el "Institut Néel") but also to a lesser extent the [Institut des sciences de la Terre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Institut_des_sciences_de_la_Terre?action=edit&redlink=1 "Institut des sciences de la Terre (page does not exist)") (part of the [Observatoire des Sciences de l'Univers de Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Observatoire_des_Sciences_de_l'Univers_de_Grenoble "Observatoire des Sciences de l'Univers de Grenoble")).

Local institutions and research organizations have united to create the [GIANT](https://www.giant-grenoble.org/en/presentation/) (Grenoble Innovation for Advanced New Technologies) Campus[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-65) with the aim at becoming a top campus in research (CEA, CNRS), higher education (INP-UGA, Grenoble Ecole de Management), and high tech.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-66)

The city benefits from the highest concentration of strategic jobs in France after Paris, with 14% of the employments, 35,186 jobs, 45% of which specialized in design and research.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-67) Grenoble is also the largest research center in France after Paris with 22,800 jobs (11,800 in public research, 7,500 in private research and 3,500 PhD students).[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble#cite_note-68)

Grenoble is also renowned for the excellence of its academic research in humanities and political sciences.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Its universities, alongside public scientific institutions, host some of the largest research centres in France (in fields such as political science, urban planning or the [sociology of organizations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sociology_of_organizations "Sociology of organizations")).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
