### Overview

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Overview")]

The museum is composed of five floors with the convent's former chapel and the nun's choir occupying the lower ground level. The ground floor includes a reception area, a series of temporary exhibition spaces, the cloister and the terraced gardens. The first floor also holds temporary exhibition spaces. The second floor is reserved for long-term exhibitions and the third floor is currently occupied by a permanent exhibition dedicated to the history of [winter sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winter_sports "Winter sports") in the region.

The museum offers three permanent exhibitions and further organises two temporary exhibitions These exhibitions are accompanied by a series of events centred around sculpture and live performances (theatre, dance, story-telling and various concerts — [baroque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baroque_music "Baroque music"), [classical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_music "Classical music"), [world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_music "World music"), contemporary music as well as [jazz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jazz "Jazz") — are regularly held in the Visitation Chapel), conferences and documentary screenings. Each exhibition is also the subject of a publication. A full catalogue of these publications can be found on the museum's [website](https://musees.isere.fr/musee/musee-dauphinois).

### Permanent Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Permanent Exhibitions")]

Following the footsteps of Jean-Pierre Laurent, the _Musée dauphinois_ seeks to display a variety of exhibitions encompassing many different topics. It offers three permanent exhibitions: _Alpins 7000 ans d'histoires, Le réve blanc,_ and _Sainte-Marie d'en Haut Il y a quatre siècles._

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5e/Expo_Le_r%C3%AAve_blanc.jpg/330px-Expo_Le_r%C3%AAve_blanc.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Expo_Le_r%C3%AAve_blanc.jpg)

The permanent exhibition _Le rêve blanc._

The museum offers three permanent exhibitions. _Alpins 7000 ans d'histoires_ first opened in 1998 and was remodelled in 2006; it displays hundreds of ethnographic items from the daily life of people living in the mountains. _Le rêve blanc_ replaced the previous permanent exhibition _La Grande Histoire du ski_ in April 2018.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois#cite_note-22) The exhibition _Sainte-Marie d'en-Haut Il y a quatre siècles_ explores the history of the former convent and chapel.

#### _Alpins, 7000 ans d'histoire_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Alpins, 7000 ans d'histoire")]

Initially titled _"Gens de là-haut_ " by Jean-Pierre Laurent and subsequently, "_Gens de l'alpe_ " in 1998, this exhibition has been readapted under the title "_Alpins, 7000 ans d'histoires_ " since 2023. It concerns settlement of the region since the [Neolithic Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") and also sheds light on daily life in the 19th and 20th centuries, including topics such as [pastoralism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastoralism "Pastoralism"), field labor, education, family structures, and community interactions, particularly within the religious sphere. Incorporating the latest research on the Alps as well as modern scenographic techniques, this exhibition explores how inhabitants have adapted to geographic, political, and socioeconomic challenges. Accessible to a wide audience, the exhibition promises an educational and engaging experience, integrating the designs of Flore Hénocque, as well as the Incoll'Alps trivia quiz, available in both French and English.

#### _Le rêve blanc_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Le rêve blanc")]

The second exhibition, titled "_Le rêve blanc. L'épopée des sports d'hiver dans les Alpes_ " reports on contemporary interactions with the Alps as well as the changes they have sparked. It simultaneously explores the [history of skiing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_skiing "History of skiing") in the region but also invites reflection on the role of the mountain and its inhabitants in the face of the climate crisis. Through a series of filmed testimonies, it offers varied perspectives and possible solutions to sustain the region's sporting tradition in light of contemporary challenges. For its reopening in 2023, one of the 33 torches from the 1968 Olympic flame was integrated into the museum's collection.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois#cite_note-23)

### Temporary Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Temporary Exhibitions")]

From 1990 to 2020, the museum has welcomed over 100 temporary expositions. As of late, it averages three new expositions per year. Several recurring themes can be found in these expositions.

*   **Archaeological heritage (regional, prehistoric, or historic):** "Premiers alpins"; "Nos villages ont cinq mille ans"; "Premiers princes [celtes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts")"; "Chevaliers de l'an mil"
*   **Industrial Heritage:** "Cathédrales électriques"; "Les Maîtres de l'acier"; "Fait main. Quand Grenoble gantait [le monde](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Monde "Le Monde")"
*   **Intangible Heritage:** "Inventer le monde, les Rhônalpins et leurs langages"; "Peurs bleues, l'enfant et les croque-mitaines"; "L'ivresse des sommets. Eaux de vie et autres breuvages des Alpes"
*   **Art:** "Rose Valland. En quête de l'art spolié"; "Bretelles et fabulations"; "Art et science"

The museum accords particular importance to immigrant communities contributing to regional culture as well as to societal themes, testified through the following expositions and publications: "La Différence" (with the _Musée d'éthnographie de Neuchâtel_ and the _Musée de la Civilisation de Québec_); "Les Millénaires de Dieu"; and "Rester libres!"

## Publications

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Publications")]

### _Le Monde alpin et rhodanien_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Le Monde alpin et rhodanien")]

A regional journal on ethnology, _Le Monde alpin et rhodanien_ published two to four issues per year from 1973 to 2006. It featured studies and articles on Southeastern France, especially on important geographical landmarks such as the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps"), the [Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rh%C3%B4ne "Rhône"), the historical [Lyonnais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyonnais "Lyonnais") province, the [Po Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Po_Valley "Po Valley"), [Lake Geneva](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lake_Geneva "Lake Geneva"), and the [Camargue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Camargue "Camargue") region. Founded in 1973 by Charles Joisten, the journal was edited by _le Centre alpin et rhodanien d'ethnologie (CARE)_, an association closely affiliated with the _Musée dauphinois._ CARE published a collection of works titled _Documents d'ethnologie régionale._ Remembrance and cultural heritage are among the central themes in interactions with the communities of the region—whether rural, urban, historical, or contemporary. The journal also examines the beliefs, rites, customs, language, oral traditions, and music of the region. [Ethnologists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnology "Ethnology"), historians, and linguists work closely with the editorial team. However, particular importance is placed on firsthand accounts, including from "self-taught" experts on the region's history and culture. These accounts offer fresh and irreplaceable perspectives on "lived" experiences, shedding light on aspects of "traditional" life. For the _Musée dauphinois,_ this journal was a key tool for disseminating scientific information about local communities and their heritage.

### _L'Alpe_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=22 "Edit section: L'Alpe")]

Proposed by André Pitte in the 1990s and born from the friendship he shared with publisher Jacques Glénat and Jean Guibal, then director of the _Musée dauphinois_, the journal _L'Alpe_ has been published quarterly since 1998. It concerns "those men who from [Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provence "Provence") to [Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Austria "Austria"), from the [Swiss Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swiss_Alps "Swiss Alps") to [Slovenia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenia "Slovenia"), have adapted to an exceptional environment and have taken advantage of the mountain, writing history composed of exchanges, migrations, and opportunities." While founded on rigorous research, _L'Alpe_ is not a scholarly journal. Leveraging the fields of history, geography, archaeology, ethnology, and literature, it seeks to connect with a broad audience in search of cultural connection, utilizing the museum's network and resources. In return, _L'Alpe_ documents the Euro-Alpine influence on the museum.

### _Les Patrimoines_

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=23 "Edit section: Les Patrimoines")]

Published by the regional newspaper _[Le Dauphiné libéré](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le\_Dauphin%C3%A9\_lib%C3%A9r%C3%A9 "Le Dauphiné libéré")_ (circulated throughout the French Alps but also in [Drôme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr%C3%B4me "Drôme"), [Ardèche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ard%C3%A8che "Ardèche"), and to the north of [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère")), _Les Patrimoines_ is a collection seeking to promote regional heritage. It highlights popular cultural sites, regional cities, famous historical figures, and local products. These publications are concise, totaling fifty pages, but highly informative, as they are compiled by specialists. The collection's wide success can be further attributed to its readability, accessibility, and the quality of the iconography in these smaller books. Over a hundred works have been published since 1998 and over a million copies have been sold. The collection's distribution perfectly compliments the mission of an institution such as the _Musée dauphinois,_ dedicated to preserving and celebrating regional heritage and history.

## Directions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_dauphinois&action=edit&section=26 "Edit section: Directions")]

*   By public transport: Bus route 40.
*   By car: Rue _Maurice-Gignoux_ leads from the quai Perrière and ascends the Bastille hill to the museum. It is worth mentioning that this road is the only naturally sloping road in the city.
*   By foot: Climb the steps of the Montée _Chalemont,_ starting at Place de la Cymaise opposite the Saint-Laurent bridge in the neighbourhood of Saint-Laurent.

The Ancien Evêché Museum entrance

The **Musée de l'Ancien Évêché** (Museum of the Former Bishopric) is a departmental museum located in Grenoble, France and dedicated to the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère") heritage through the history of its Bishop's palace. Inaugurated in 1998,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9#cite_note-1) it is settled in the former Bishop's palace, near [Grenoble Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Cathedral "Grenoble Cathedral"). The museum gives access to the remains of an early Christian baptistry and to a section of the [vestiges of the Gallo-Roman wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestiges_of_the_Gallo-Roman_wall,_Grenoble "Vestiges of the Gallo-Roman wall, Grenoble") in the basement of the building.

## Permanent exhibition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_de_l%27Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Permanent exhibition")]

The permanent exhibition _Isère through History_ displays items and paintings relating to the development of Isère from pre-history to the present day. The museum also shows regularly temporary exhibitions of local artists.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9#cite_note-2) In December 2014, a public garden was inaugurated near the entrance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9#cite_note-3)

The **Musée de l'Ancien Évêché** (Museum of the Former Bishopric) is a departmental museum located in Grenoble, France and dedicated to the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère") heritage through the history of its Bishop's palace. Inaugurated in 1998,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9#cite_note-1) it is settled in the former Bishop's palace, near [Grenoble Cathedral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenoble_Cathedral "Grenoble Cathedral"). The museum gives access to the remains of an early Christian baptistry and to a section of the [vestiges of the Gallo-Roman wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vestiges_of_the_Gallo-Roman_wall,_Grenoble "Vestiges of the Gallo-Roman wall, Grenoble") in the basement of the building.

## Permanent exhibition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Mus%C3%A9e_de_l%27Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Permanent exhibition")]

The permanent exhibition _Isère through History_ displays items and paintings relating to the development of Isère from pre-history to the present day. The museum also shows regularly temporary exhibitions of local artists.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9#cite_note-2) In December 2014, a public garden was inaugurated near the entrance.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_l'Ancien_%C3%89v%C3%AAch%C3%A9#cite_note-3)

The **Museum of Grenoble** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Musée de Grenoble_) is a municipal museum of [Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_Arts "Fine Arts") and antiquities in the city of Grenoble in the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère") region of France.

Located on the left bank of the [Isère River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)"), place Lavalette, it is known both for its collections of ancient art and for its collections of modern and contemporary art.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-2) Thanks to the action of [Andry-Farcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andry-Farcy "Andry-Farcy"), one of its curators in the [interwar period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interwar_period "Interwar period"), it is considered the very best museum of [modern art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_art "Modern art") in France.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-3)

Its temporary rooms allow it to organize two exhibitions each year.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Louis-Joseph_Jay_par_Jacques-Augustin_Pajou.gif/250px-Louis-Joseph_Jay_par_Jacques-Augustin_Pajou.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Louis-Joseph_Jay_par_Jacques-Augustin_Pajou.gif)

Louis-Joseph Jay

The Museum of Grenoble was founded on 16 February 1798 by Louis-Joseph Jay, well before other French provincial museums.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-4) That day, an order of the local administration detailed the creation of a _museum_ in Grenoble, in which article 10 stipulated that «the citizen Louis-Joseph Jay is appointed curator of this museum.»[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-5)

In May of that year, the [Interior Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_minister "Interior minister") canceled the creation of the museum but a provisional authorization was obtained in December, which became final on 3 April 1800. Beginning in 1799, while engaged in collecting works of art of the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère") Region, Jay requested a public subscription to purchase paintings and drawings.

Housed in four halls of the first floor of the former bishopric from its opening on 31 December 1800, the museum had 298 works of art including 177 paintings, 80 drawings or engravings and 45 sculptures placed in the garden. Each hall had a name, the first Hall of Apollo, was devoted to French painters, the second Hall of Castor and Pollux, was devoted to Italian and French schools, the third Salon of Gladiator, had copies of the life of [San Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_of_Cologne "Bruno of Cologne") by [Eustache Lesueur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustache_Lesueur "Eustache Lesueur"), and the last hall was called Hall of the Venus de Medici, displaying the art of the Flemish school. A few months after its opening, the [Concordat of 1801](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concordat_of_1801 "Concordat of 1801") by [Napoleon Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_Bonaparte "Napoleon Bonaparte") forced the evacuation of the premises of the museum to restore them to their original purpose.

So in this way it was relocated on 14 July 1802, into the Central School,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-6) which is currently the Stendhall School ([Lycée Stendhal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Stendhal "Lycée Stendhal")). On 12 March 1807, a decree transformed the museum from a county museum into a municipal museum.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-7) On 15 February 1811, an imperial decree allocated 209 paintings to six French cities and gave 32 to Grenoble.

In 1815, despite a partial dispersion of works as a result of the _[Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second\_Restoration "Second Restoration")_, (57 paintings were returned to their owners, 11 disappeared and an unknown number were deposited in the churches) the collection continued to increase. The acquisitions, donations and legacies continued throughout the 19th century, and made it essential to construct a new building despite there having been a building expansion in 1844.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Ancien_mus%C3%A9e-biblioth%C3%A8que_-_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Ancien_mus%C3%A9e-biblioth%C3%A8que_-_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ancien_mus%C3%A9e-biblioth%C3%A8que_-_Grenoble.JPG)

Former museum-library.

A new building designed by the architect [Charles-Auguste Questel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles-Auguste_Questel "Charles-Auguste Questel") was inaugurated in 1870, on the current site of Verdun Square. The museum-library, so called because it also housed the _Municipal Library of Grenoble_, is one of the great examples of museum architecture in France and Europe.

Towards the end of the 19th century, a major patron, General [Leon de Beylié](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_de_Beyli%C3%A9?action=edit&redlink=1 "Leon de Beylié (page does not exist)") added to the museum's collection by donating four famous paintings by [Francisco de Zurbarán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Zurbar%C3%A1n "Francisco de Zurbarán"), continuing a long tradition of donations and bequests. De Beylié had a direct and massive influence on the wealth and the nature of the collections. From 1895 until his accidental death on 15 July 1910, he bought for the museum 50 paintings, 13 drawings, 16 sculptures, 13 pieces of archeology and hundreds of objects from the Far East.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-8)

From 1920 to the early-1950s, the Museum of Grenoble was considered the premier museum of contemporary art in France, since the Paris museum did not open until 1947. It was even one of the first museums in the world, together with the [_Folkwang Museum_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_Folkwang "Museum Folkwang") in [Essen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essen "Essen") (Germany) and the _Muzeum Sztuki_ in [Łódź](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81%C3%B3d%C5%BA "Łódź") (Poland), as well as the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") in New York which did not open until 1929.

In 1982, President [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand") announced a plan to construct a new building. The following year, the new mayor of Grenoble Alain Carignon, and the Minister of Culture [Jack Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lang_(French_politician) "Jack Lang (French politician)"), agreed on the idea and on the site of the new building, on a parking lot near the centre of town. After the selection of architects in 1987, construction began in 1990.

On January 30, 1994, the new building housing the collections was inaugurated by Prime Minister [Édouard Balladur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Balladur "Édouard Balladur"). Located in the heart of the city, bordering the [Isère River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)"), it tripled the exhibition space of the old museum. Its total cost was 203 million French francs (31 million euros). To complete the Museum there is a sculpture garden in the Albert Michallon park, a wooded area of 16,000 m 2 surrounding the old city wall from the late 19th century.

## History of the location of the new museum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History of the location of the new museum")]

The current location of the museum was occupied since the 13th century by the great monastery of the [Brothers Minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Friars_Minor "Order of Friars Minor"), known in France as the Cordeliers or [Franciscans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans") until they moved to the current Berulle Square in 1592.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-9) Integrated into the city in the 13th century by an extension of the Roman wall, the place was at the eastern extremity of the town and remained so until the 19th century, while different generations of fortifications were built over the centuries.

Thus was built the Tower of the Island in 1401, serving as a defence system that allowed relative autonomy for the consuls of the city who considered it to be their main "home City". In 1591, the future [Duke of Lesdiguieres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Bonne,_duc_de_Lesdigui%C3%A8res "François de Bonne, duc de Lesdiguières"), who came to take possession of the city during the religious wars, built a new fortified wall, turning the place into a small fortress called _Arsenal_ to protect himself from any rebellion of the inhabitants. In this way the area became the first barracks in the history of the city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-10)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Mur_d%27enceinte_1888_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Mur_d%27enceinte_1888_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mur_d'enceinte_1888_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG)

The 1888 Wall in the museum

In the 19th century, General [Haxo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Nicolas_Beno%C3%AEt,_Baron_Haxo "François Nicolas Benoît, Baron Haxo") enlarged the precincts of the city from 1832 to 1836 by building a new fortification wall close to the _Arsenal_. Historically a place of military occupation, the area was occupied during the 19th century by several barracks of which Vinoy barracks was on the site of the museum and the Bizanet barracks was opposite. [_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Around 1888, a change was made to the Haxo wall.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-11) At the urging of the mayor, Edouard Rey, and the population, the engineer created a new gate, the Gate of _Saulaie_ to serve the new district of [Green Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Ele_Verte_(Grenoble) "Île Verte (Grenoble)"). This new gate obliged the military for technical reasons to correct the path of the Haxo wall, building a new line of wall square to the old wall down to the edge of the [Isère River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)") at the site of an old [Ravelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravelin "Ravelin") fortification. This new wall of 150 linear meters has been preserved from the sculpture garden to the football field then going through part of the structure of the Museum. In 1967 the [Vinoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Vinoy "Joseph Vinoy") barracks were demolished, leaving room for a large parking lot.

## Architecture building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Architecture building")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Hall_d%27accueil_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Hall_d%27accueil_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hall_d'accueil_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG)

Lobby of the museum

The present building of 18,270 sq.m.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-12) was inaugurated in 1994 as part of a program of large works in the province initiated in 1982. It was designed by architects Olivier Félix-Faure, Antoine Félix-Faure and Philippe Macary from the architectural firm from Grenoble _Groupe6_, assisted by museographer Lorenzo Piqueras.

On the site there were severe design constraints. The imperatives were in respect to the immediate vicinity of the site. To the North-west a part of the Lesdiguieres wall dating from 1591 are recorded as being historical monuments. Nearby, the _Tower of the Island_ dating from 1401, is also a register structure. To the east, the modified part of the wall built around 1888 must be conserved, forcing the integration of part of it inside the building. Finally to the east, access to a football stadium must to be retained during the development of the structure for an area with high urban population density.

The museum is built over a huge parking lot on three levels keeping it safe from flooding from the Isère River.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-13) For the exhibition areas, the museum itself is built on three levels, but most of the display halls are located at level 0. At this level, the halls are served by a wide central aisle. On the left are the five sequences of ancient art, on the right are temporary exhibitions. The end of the aisle has been left empty of any work, in an arc, this huge area is dedicated to the 20th century, and also gives access to the Tower of the Island.

Levels -1 and -2 are smaller floors, and thus have a limited number of rooms. Their lighting is no longer an overhead light useful for study as in the halls of level 0. At level-1 has installed after the lobby, three rooms of Greek, Etruscan and Egyptian antiquities, and at the other end of the building, four rooms covering art at the end of the 20th century (after 1960). Below, level-2 has six rooms for the 21st century. It is also at this level that leads to the spectacular integration of the end of the 19th century wall into this futuristic building.

A few metres from the building, the museum features via a skywalk of glass and steel, the Tower of the Island, transforming it into a place of exhibition graphics. The architecture also incorporates the district football stadium into the complex.

Inside, the transitions between levels are equipped with wide ramps and three lifts to travel between floors. The rooms are designed to rest the eye: uniform wooden floors, white walls, etc.

Around the cylindrical entry hall, are the reception counter, library, shop, and cafeteria. Upstairs museum offices, as well as those of the Association of Friends of the Museum, the Association of Museum in Music, which organizes concerts in an auditorium of 275 seats in partnership with [The Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Louvre "The Louvre") and finally the André Chastel library equipped with a specialized collection of 55,000 art history books available to consult on site.

## Museum curators

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Museum curators")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Alexandre_Debelle_by_Jacques_Gay_-_1881.jpg/250px-Alexandre_Debelle_by_Jacques_Gay_-_1881.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexandre_Debelle_by_Jacques_Gay_-_1881.jpg)

[Alexandre Debelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Debelle "Alexandre Debelle"), curator from 1853 to 1887. Portrait by [Jacques Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Gay "Jacques Gay")

Two Curators have made a special mark on the history of the museum: Louis-Joseph Jay and Andry-Farcy. The first created and ensured the implementation of the museum from 1798 to 1815,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-14) before leaving the estate to Benjamin Rolland. Painters [Alexandre Debelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Debelle "Alexandre Debelle") and Jules Bernard ensured the succession as preservationists.

Then during the 20th century, there were Xavier Borgey and in particular Pierre André Farcy, called Andry-Farcy, curator from 1919 to 1949, who decisively guided the museum in favour of the collection of modern art. He left but agreed to come back in exchange for the promise of displaying a number of contemporary works by Matisse, Picasso and Monnet beside some of the great works of the museum. This caused a violent press campaign against him. His opponents would come to name his art gallery, the "rigolarium" [comedy house]. His successors were Jean Leymarie, Gabrielle Kueny, Maurice Besset, [Marie-Claude Beaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Claude_Beaud "Marie-Claude Beaud"), [Pierre Gaudibert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Gaudibert "Pierre Gaudibert"), Hélène Vincent (Temporary for 2 years), Serge Lemoine, [Guy Tosatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Tosatto "Guy Tosatto"), and since 2024 Sebastien Gokalp[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-15).

## Collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Collections")]

The museum offers the possibility of following without interruption western history from the 13th to the 21st century, with each period represented by first rank works of art. Less known to the general public, as a parenthesis to the main course, there is a collection of 115 African statues and artifacts[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-17) are in the aisle between the 19th and the 20th century. The visitor has the opportunity to use an audio guide for a fee that allows him to view the collections at his own pace. The commentaries are recorded by actors and are short and lively. The permanent collections altogether consist of 1,500 works in 57 rooms of 14,000 m 2 which are grouped as follows:

### Ancient Egyptian, Greek and Roman

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Ancient Egyptian, Greek and Roman")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1e/Salle_sarcophages_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Salle_sarcophages_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salle_sarcophages_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG)

Room 59. Sarcophagi Egyptology section

Two rooms are located off the lobby, the level-1 is devoted to antiquities from [ancient Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Egypt "Ancient Egypt"), with particularly beautiful [sarcophagi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarcophagus "Sarcophagus"). One room is devoted to Roman antiquities, and another room to Greek antiquities. The city of Grenoble is linked to the story of [Champollion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_Champollion "Jean-François Champollion") and that of Egyptology.

From the 18th century, there are ancient Egyptian pieces from excavations run by the antiques office of the municipal library of Grenoble, of which [Jean-François Champollion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_Champollion "Jean-François Champollion") was the assistant librarian. It is natural that the collection found in the museum has not ceased to be enriched by many gifts in the 19th, and early 20th centuries.

Most important discoveries have been made by the French Society during archaeological excavations conducted in 1907 and 1913, following the excavation of Antinoöpolis, of Touna-el-Gebel, and of Kom el Ahmar, and later by the family of Count Saint-Ferriol in 1916. In April 2010, the "_prophétesse d'Antinoé_", a 6th-century mummy discovered in 1907, in a [Coptic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Copts "Copts")[necropolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Necropolis "Necropolis") at [Antinoöpolis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antinopolis "Antinopolis") in Middle Egypt, was returned to the Museum of Grenoble, after more than fifty years of absence.

The collection of ancient Egyptian antiquities is regarded as the fifth largest in France, after that of the [Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louvre "Louvre"), the Museum of Archeology Mediterranean in Marseille, [Lyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_des_Beaux-Arts_de_Lyon "Musée des Beaux-Arts de Lyon"), and [Dijon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_des_Beaux-Arts_de_Dijon "Musée des Beaux-Arts de Dijon"). It includes furniture and funerary objects of everyday life. The entire tomb is impressive, especially the fragmentary tomb of Amenhotep son of Hapu, vizier of [Amenhotep III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amenhotep_III "Amenhotep III").

A third room of antiquities contains an interesting collection of Greek and Etruscan ceramic statues.

### 13th to 16th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 13th to 16th century")]

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cc/Salle_N%C2%B01_XIII-XVIe_si%C3%A8cle_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Salle_N%C2%B01_XIII-XVIe_si%C3%A8cle_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salle_N%C2%B01_XIII-XVIe_si%C3%A8cle_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG)

Room 1, 13th century

The collection begins with the origins of Western painting, then quickly reaches the period of [Renaissance art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance_art "Renaissance art").

*   _Santa Lucia_ assigned to [Jacopo Torriti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacopo_Torriti "Jacopo Torriti")
*   Three part work: _The Virgin and Child with St. Gerard, St. Paul, St. Andrew and St. Nicolas_ (1395) by [Taddeo di Bartolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taddeo_di_Bartolo "Taddeo di Bartolo")
*   _Christ meeting a woman and the sons of Zebedee_ and _[Noli me tangere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Noli\_me\_tangere\_(Veronese)?action=edit&redlink=1 "Noli me tangere (Veronese) (page does not exist)")_ by [Veronese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Veronese "Paul Veronese")
*   _The statue of Hercules_ a bronze dating from the 16th century and made by the sculptor Jacob Richier in the 17th century, a copy is placed in the centre of the _City Garden_ at the Hôtel de Lesdiguières in Grenoble.

Works of Pérugin (2 paintings), [Fra Bartolomeo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fra_Bartolomeo "Fra Bartolomeo") (attributed to), [Giorgio Vasari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_Vasari "Giorgio Vasari"), [Adrien Ysenbrandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrien_Ysenbrandt "Adrien Ysenbrandt"), and [Georg Pencz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georg_Pencz "Georg Pencz") can also be found in this section.

The works of this century are presented in the majestic grand format of the French school, such as _Martyrdom of St Andrew_ painted in 1749 by [Jean Restout](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_II_Restout "Jean II Restout") for the [collegiate Church of Saint-André in Grenoble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collegiate_Church_of_Saint-Andr%C3%A9,_Grenoble "Collegiate Church of Saint-André, Grenoble").

*   _The Point of the Customs at Venice_[Canaletto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canaletto "Canaletto")
*   _The Doge of Venice carried by the gondoliers_ by [Francesco Guardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Guardi "Francesco Guardi").
*   _Animals flowers and fruit_, painted in 1717 by [François Desportes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Desportes "François Desportes")
*   _Snowy Landscape with rocks and Travelers_ painted around 1750 by [Francesco Foschi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Foschi "Francesco Foschi")
*   _Roger arriving in Alcine Island_, 1740 by [Hyacinthe Collin de Vermont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyacinthe_Collin_de_Vermont "Hyacinthe Collin de Vermont") (One of the largest paintings in the museum)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-18)

Other paintings are notably by: [Nicolas de Largilliere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_de_Largilliere "Nicolas de Largilliere"), [Hyacinthe Rigaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyacinthe_Rigaud "Hyacinthe Rigaud"), [Jean-Baptiste Greuze](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Greuze "Jean-Baptiste Greuze"), [Joseph-Marie Vien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph-Marie_Vien "Joseph-Marie Vien"), [Sebastiano Ricci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sebastiano_Ricci "Sebastiano Ricci"), [Giovanni Paolo Pannini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Paolo_Pannini "Giovanni Paolo Pannini"), and [Thomas Gainsborough](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Gainsborough "Thomas Gainsborough"). This section also displays many busts by [Antoine Barnave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoine_Barnave "Antoine Barnave").

In room 17, is a plaster 2 metres high of [Jean-François Champollion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Fran%C3%A7ois_Champollion "Jean-François Champollion") by the sculptor [Bartholdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fr%C3%A9d%C3%A9ric_Auguste_Bartholdi "Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi"). This plaster has served as a model for the marble sculpture at the [Collège de France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coll%C3%A8ge_de_France "Collège de France") in Paris.

### Regional art of the 19th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Regional art of the 19th century")]

The Dauphinoise school of the 19th century, reached a level that justifies the prominence it holds in the museum. If a large room displays these small paintings it is above all this landscape format that gives them their soul. The founder of this school, [Jean Achard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Achard_(painter) "Jean Achard (painter)") created the first majestic landscapes that excited the painters that followed: [Laurent Guétal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_Gu%C3%A9tal "Laurent Guétal"), [Charles Bertier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Bertier "Charles Bertier"), [Ernest Hébert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ernest_H%C3%A9bert "Ernest Hébert"), the Abbe Cales. Many of these painters, despite the topographical precision required, thought it an inspired vision.

### 20th century

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: 20th century")]

Rooms from 24 to 48[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b4/Partie_XXe_si%C3%A8cle_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_grenoble.JPG/250px-Partie_XXe_si%C3%A8cle_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Partie_XXe_si%C3%A8cle_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_grenoble.JPG)

Room 36 of the 20th century collection

The section of the 20th century is particularly rich because the museum is considered the oldest museum of contemporary art in France.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-19)

Spread over more than twenty rooms, the collection covers modern art from the beginning of the century to the most recent formal developments. Part of the collection comes from the important legacy of [Agutte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgette_Agutte "Georgette Agutte")[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-20) – [Sembat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Sembat "Marcel Sembat"). All the trends and movements of the painter are present, such as [Fauvism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fauvism "Fauvism") with the paintings of [Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse") (8 paintings), [André Derain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Derain "André Derain"), [Albert Marquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Marquet "Albert Marquet"), [Raoul Dufy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raoul_Dufy "Raoul Dufy"), [Maurice de Vlaminck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_de_Vlaminck "Maurice de Vlaminck"), [Emile Othon Friesz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Othon_Friesz "Othon Friesz") (6 pictures), [Jean Puy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Puy "Jean Puy"), [Charles Camoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Camoin "Charles Camoin") (Nude with purple shirt, acquired in 2012), and [Kees van Dongen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kees_van_Dongen "Kees van Dongen"). [Cubism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubism "Cubism") with [Georges Braque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Braque "Georges Braque"), [Albert Gleizes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Albert_Gleizes "Albert Gleizes") and [Fernand Léger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernand_L%C3%A9ger "Fernand Léger"). The School of Paris, represented by [Amedeo Modigliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amedeo_Modigliani "Amedeo Modigliani"), [Chaïm Soutine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cha%C3%AFm_Soutine "Chaïm Soutine"), [Maurice Utrillo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurice_Utrillo "Maurice Utrillo"), and [Chagall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chagall "Chagall"). Four paintings illustrate the different artistic periods of [Pablo Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Picasso "Pablo Picasso") while there are also works of painters such as [Pierre Bonnard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Bonnard "Pierre Bonnard"), [Jacques Villon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Villon "Jacques Villon"), [Natalia Goncharova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natalia_Goncharova "Natalia Goncharova"), [Paul Signac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Signac "Paul Signac"), [Henri-Edmond Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri-Edmond_Cross "Henri-Edmond Cross") (5 paintings), [Claude Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claude_Monet "Claude Monet"), [Georges Rouault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Rouault "Georges Rouault"), [Robert Delaunay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Delaunay "Robert Delaunay"), [Kurt Schwitters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurt_Schwitters "Kurt Schwitters"), [George Grosz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Grosz "George Grosz"), [Paul Klee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Klee "Paul Klee"), [Wassily Kandinsky](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wassily_Kandinsky "Wassily Kandinsky"), [František Kupka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franti%C5%A1ek_Kupka "František Kupka"), [Theo van Doesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theo_van_Doesburg "Theo van Doesburg"), [Jean Arp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Arp "Jean Arp"), [Nicolas de Staël](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolas_de_Sta%C3%ABl "Nicolas de Staël"), [Balthus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balthus "Balthus"), [Bernard Buffet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Buffet "Bernard Buffet") and [Hans Hartung](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Hartung "Hans Hartung").

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4b/Henri_Matisse%2C_1906%2C_Le_Tapis_rouge%2C_Int%C3%A9rieur_au_tapis_rouge%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_89_x_116_cm%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg/250px-Henri_Matisse%2C_1906%2C_Le_Tapis_rouge%2C_Int%C3%A9rieur_au_tapis_rouge%2C_oil_on_canvas%2C_89_x_116_cm%2C_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Henri_Matisse,_1906,_Le_Tapis_rouge,_Int%C3%A9rieur_au_tapis_rouge,_oil_on_canvas,_89_x_116_cm,_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg)

[Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse"), 1906, _Le Tapis rouge, Intérieur au tapis rouge_, oil on canvas, 89 x 116 cm

[Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matisse "Matisse") donated his _Interior of eggplants_, Pablo Picasso's _Woman reading_ in 1921 Claude Monet's _Corner of the pond at Giverny_ in 1923. Great names of surrealism are also present such as [Giorgio de Chirico](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giorgio_de_Chirico "Giorgio de Chirico"), [René Magritte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ren%C3%A9_Magritte "René Magritte"), [Joan Miró](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_Mir%C3%B3 "Joan Miró"), [Max Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ernst "Max Ernst"), [André Masson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Masson "André Masson"), [Francis Picabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Picabia "Francis Picabia"), and [Yves Tanguy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yves_Tanguy "Yves Tanguy"). Sculptures are also present in some rooms with works of [Auguste Rodin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auguste_Rodin "Auguste Rodin"), [Georges Rouault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georges_Rouault "Georges Rouault")(_female nude_, c.1909), [Henri Laurens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Laurens "Henri Laurens"), [Raymond Duchamp-Villon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raymond_Duchamp-Villon "Raymond Duchamp-Villon"), [Jacques Lipchitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Lipchitz "Jacques Lipchitz"), [Julio Gonzalez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Gonz%C3%A1lez_(sculptor) "Julio González (sculptor)"), [Ossip Zadkine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossip_Zadkine "Ossip Zadkine"), [Max Ernst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Ernst "Max Ernst") (_A lost Chinaman_), [Alberto Giacometti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Giacometti "Alberto Giacometti"), [Alexander Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder"), and even [Henri Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henri_Matisse "Henri Matisse"), again thanks to the Agutte-Sembat legacy.

The Museum of Grenoble is also a reference for contemporary art, its collection is one of the oldest in France, including works by [Pierre Soulages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Soulages "Pierre Soulages"), [Christian Boltanski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christian_Boltanski "Christian Boltanski") (_Monument_), [Christo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christo "Christo"), [Tàpies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antoni_T%C3%A0pies "Antoni Tàpies"), [Andy Warhol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andy_Warhol "Andy Warhol"), [Donald Judd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Judd "Donald Judd"), [Robert Ryman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Ryman "Robert Ryman"), [Jean Dubuffet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Dubuffet "Jean Dubuffet"), Jean Peyrissac, [Annette Messager](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annette_Messager "Annette Messager") and [Rebecca Horn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rebecca_Horn "Rebecca Horn").

In 2012, the Museum of Grenoble acquired one of the thirteen pinned cubist collages of [Pablo Picasso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pablo_Picasso "Pablo Picasso") dated Spring 1914. Acquired for an amount of 750,000 euros thanks to the patrons club of the museum, "Glass" will be presented for three years for two-month periods starting from 19 December 2012.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-21)

### 21st century

Rooms from 49 to 54
The last rooms located on level-2 are devoted to the present century. They highlight the great diversity of forms and concerns explored by the creators of today using diverse materials, techniques and inspiration.

The _Blue Head_ by [Thomas Schutte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thomas_Schutte "Thomas Schutte") is characteristic of this diversity.

### Drawings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Drawings")]

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/31/Paul_Gauguin%2C_Te_nave_nave_fenua_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg/250px-Paul_Gauguin%2C_Te_nave_nave_fenua_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paul_Gauguin,_Te_nave_nave_fenua_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg)

_Te nave nave fenua_, [Paul Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), 1892. Drawing of his Tahitian period where he represents his companion, _Teha'amana_. (painting is in [Ohara Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ohara_Museum_of_Art "Ohara Museum of Art"), Japan)

Most often displayed in the _Tower if the Island_, arranged into an exhibition of graphic arts, the old collection consists of 5,500 drawings[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-22) mainly from donations and bequests of Léonce Mesnard in the 19th century. He will devote part of his life to his writings and collections. At his death in May 1890, the Mayor of Grenoble, Auguste Gache, gave a eulogy on his great generosity in leaving 3,207 items to the Museum.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-23)

Italian drawings predominate, especially the Venetians, and the Florentines of the Renaissance and of [Seicento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seicento "Seicento") although there are also many other single drawings. The Museum owns drawings by: [Parmigianino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parmigianino "Parmigianino") (Parmesan), [Palma the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palma_the_Younger "Palma the Younger"), [Annibale Carracci](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annibale_Carracci "Annibale Carracci"), [Agostino Ciampelli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agostino_Ciampelli "Agostino Ciampelli"), [Guido Reni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guido_Reni "Guido Reni"), [Guercino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guercino "Guercino"), [Luca Giordano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luca_Giordano "Luca Giordano"), [Giambattista Tiepolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giambattista_Tiepolo "Giambattista Tiepolo"), [Giandomenico Tiepolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giandomenico_Tiepolo "Giandomenico Tiepolo"), [Francesco Guardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francesco_Guardi "Francesco Guardi"), [Giovanni Battista Piazzetta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giovanni_Battista_Piazzetta "Giovanni Battista Piazzetta") etc..

The old French drawings have recently been studied by Guillaume Kazerouni, Barbara Brejon de Lavergnée, and Jérôme Delaplanche, resulting in the publication of a catalogue and enabling new attributions through the discovery of new designs: for the 17th century, a collection of drawings was found by artists such as: [Laurent de La Hyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laurent_de_La_Hyre "Laurent de La Hyre"), [Philippe de Champaigne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippe_de_Champaigne "Philippe de Champaigne"), and [Vouet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vouet "Vouet"). The 18th century is represented by famous artists such as [Watteau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watteau "Watteau"), [Hubert Robert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Robert "Hubert Robert"), and [David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Louis_David "Jacques-Louis David"). The Dutch school stands out for its importance most notably [Jacob Jordaens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Jordaens "Jacob Jordaens") and [Rembrandt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rembrandt "Rembrandt"). The 19th century is characterized by an important series by artists such as: [Eugène Delacroix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eug%C3%A8ne_Delacroix "Eugène Delacroix"), [Paul Gauguin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Gauguin "Paul Gauguin"), [Fantin-Latour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fantin-Latour "Fantin-Latour"), and [Jongkind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jongkind "Jongkind")[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-24) with watercolors by Dauphiné.

The 20th century collection ranks second in terms of importance for a French museum after the National Museum of Modern Art. As for the paintings, they owe much to the policy of the curator Andry-Farcy. In 1923, the legacy of Agutte-Sembat brought in 24 drawings including a charcoal sketch of _The Dance_ by [Matisse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matisse "Matisse") in 1909. ## The sculpture garden

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: The sculpture garden")]

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/41/Plan_site_mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg/250px-Plan_site_mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Plan_site_mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.jpg)

Sitemap of museum.

A sculpture garden, a concept born in the 17th century, has been installed on the perimeter east / north-west of the museum, in Albert-Michallon Park.

Covering an area of 16,000 m 2, in 1964 it was the first development allowed at the location of an old half moon fortification. Overall, the park is a square shape and meets the path of the massive 19th-century fortification wall that ends inside the museum. Beautifully landscaped, this park contains the oldest tree in the city, a Cedar from Lebanon planted in 1847.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-25) It offers a unique opportunity in the heart of town to display outdoor sculptures.

The surface of the Michallon Park does not allow an unlimited area to present sculptures. In 1988, the choice of development was focused on the 20th century period, consistent with the extensive collection of the contemporary art museum. Going to the park through the front of the museum, partly framed by the walls built at the end of the 16th century by the Duke of Lesdiguieres, two works in metal and a bronze statue placed on the Esplanade François Mitterrand can be seen. These are:

*   [Alexander Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Calder "Alexander Calder") – _Monsieur Loyal_, 1993, height 9 metres, painted steel 1967
*   [Mark di Suvero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_di_Suvero "Mark di Suvero") – _Polar Star_, 23 meters high, 18 metres wide, painted steel 1972
*   [Marcel Gimond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Gimond "Marcel Gimond") – _Girl standing_, bronze 1934, (in front of the 16th century wall)

In the Albert Michallon Albert Park, some works closest to the museum, such as _Duna_, are visible from the inside. These are:

*   Robert Wlérick – _Standing Female Nude_, patinated bronze, (1936–1942)
*   [Marta Pan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marta_Pan "Marta Pan") – _Duna_ (Danube, Hungary) 1992, height 3.30 metres, 5 discs of pink granite 1991
*   [Ossip Zadkine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ossip_Zadkine "Ossip Zadkine") – _Orpheus_, bronze 1948
*   [Bernar Venet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernar_Venet "Bernar Venet") – _Three Indeterminate Lines_, 1994, [weathered steel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weathering_steel "Weathering steel") 1992
*   [Léon-Ernest Drivier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9on-Ernest_Drivier "Léon-Ernest Drivier")&[Marcel Gimond](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Gimond "Marcel Gimond") – _Cecilia_, treated antique bronze 1928
*   [George Rickey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Rickey "George Rickey") – _Conversation_ (mobile sculpture Stainless Steel) 1991
*   [Gottfried Honegger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gottfried_Honegger "Gottfried Honegger") – _Monoform 26_, height 5 metres, painted metal 1988
*   Morice Lipsi – _The Great Wave_, stone 1978
*   [Eduardo Chillida](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduardo_Chillida "Eduardo Chillida") – _Zuhaitz_ (tree), weathered steel 1989
*   [Anthony Caro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Caro "Anthony Caro") – _The Song of the mountains_, which backs on to the old wall, 1993
*   [Richard Nonas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nonas "Richard Nonas") – _Transi West (for 36 Albanians ...)_, 1994
*   [Eugene Dodeigne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugene_Dodeigne "Eugene Dodeigne") – _Couple_ Pierre de Soignies, 1993

## The Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: The Library")]

The Library of Art History is open to the public with consultation on site. Books about the collection and the policy for purchasing works of art are the most important and heavily used by students. The Library is open on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays from 2pm to 6pm. It is closed during summer.

## Temporary exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Temporary exhibitions")]

In addition to space devoted to the presentation of permanent collections, some halls with an area of 1,000 square metres are reserved for temporary exhibitions.

[![Image 33](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Bassin_d%27eau_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Bassin_d%27eau_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bassin_d'eau_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG)

The patio with a water basin.

Each year, two major exhibitions are organized to help make the museum an important centre of French artistic life. At the exit to these rooms, a pool of water encourages visitors to take a break. In 2011 there was a record attendance for a temporary exhibition with 143,230 visitors for the Chagall exhibition surpassing hugely the previous record of 98,000 visitors for the Impressionism of France and America exhibition of 2008. In 2019, the exhibition _Serving the gods of Egypt_ attracts 136,127 visitors, the second largest affluence in the history of the museum.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-26)

## International trade

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: International trade")]

The Museum of Grenoble is part of the _frame_ (_French Regional & American Museum Exchange_), one of whose missions is to promote the circulation and exchange of art between French and American museums.

The **Museum of Grenoble** ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Musée de Grenoble_) is a municipal museum of [Fine Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fine_Arts "Fine Arts") and antiquities in the city of Grenoble in the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère") region of France.

Located on the left bank of the [Isère River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)"), place Lavalette, it is known both for its collections of ancient art and for its collections of modern and contemporary art.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-2) Thanks to the action of [Andry-Farcy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andry-Farcy "Andry-Farcy"), one of its curators in the [interwar period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interwar_period "Interwar period"), it is considered the very best museum of [modern art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modern_art "Modern art") in France.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-3)

Its temporary rooms allow it to organize two exhibitions each year.

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 8](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c5/Louis-Joseph_Jay_par_Jacques-Augustin_Pajou.gif/250px-Louis-Joseph_Jay_par_Jacques-Augustin_Pajou.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Louis-Joseph_Jay_par_Jacques-Augustin_Pajou.gif)

Louis-Joseph Jay

The Museum of Grenoble was founded on 16 February 1798 by Louis-Joseph Jay, well before other French provincial museums.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-4) That day, an order of the local administration detailed the creation of a _museum_ in Grenoble, in which article 10 stipulated that «the citizen Louis-Joseph Jay is appointed curator of this museum.»[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-5)

In May of that year, the [Interior Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interior_minister "Interior minister") canceled the creation of the museum but a provisional authorization was obtained in December, which became final on 3 April 1800. Beginning in 1799, while engaged in collecting works of art of the [Isère](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re "Isère") Region, Jay requested a public subscription to purchase paintings and drawings.

Housed in four halls of the first floor of the former bishopric from its opening on 31 December 1800, the museum had 298 works of art including 177 paintings, 80 drawings or engravings and 45 sculptures placed in the garden. Each hall had a name, the first Hall of Apollo, was devoted to French painters, the second Hall of Castor and Pollux, was devoted to Italian and French schools, the third Salon of Gladiator, had copies of the life of [San Bruno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruno_of_Cologne "Bruno of Cologne") by [Eustache Lesueur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eustache_Lesueur "Eustache Lesueur"), and the last hall was called Hall of the Venus de Medici, displaying the art of the Flemish school. A few months after its opening, the [Concordat of 1801](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concordat_of_1801 "Concordat of 1801") by [Napoleon Bonaparte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_Bonaparte "Napoleon Bonaparte") forced the evacuation of the premises of the museum to restore them to their original purpose.

So in this way it was relocated on 14 July 1802, into the Central School,[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-6) which is currently the Stendhall School ([Lycée Stendhal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyc%C3%A9e_Stendhal "Lycée Stendhal")). On 12 March 1807, a decree transformed the museum from a county museum into a municipal museum.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-7) On 15 February 1811, an imperial decree allocated 209 paintings to six French cities and gave 32 to Grenoble.

In 1815, despite a partial dispersion of works as a result of the _[Restoration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second\_Restoration "Second Restoration")_, (57 paintings were returned to their owners, 11 disappeared and an unknown number were deposited in the churches) the collection continued to increase. The acquisitions, donations and legacies continued throughout the 19th century, and made it essential to construct a new building despite there having been a building expansion in 1844.

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/Ancien_mus%C3%A9e-biblioth%C3%A8que_-_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Ancien_mus%C3%A9e-biblioth%C3%A8que_-_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ancien_mus%C3%A9e-biblioth%C3%A8que_-_Grenoble.JPG)

Former museum-library.

A new building designed by the architect [Charles-Auguste Questel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles-Auguste_Questel "Charles-Auguste Questel") was inaugurated in 1870, on the current site of Verdun Square. The museum-library, so called because it also housed the _Municipal Library of Grenoble_, is one of the great examples of museum architecture in France and Europe.

Towards the end of the 19th century, a major patron, General [Leon de Beylié](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leon_de_Beyli%C3%A9?action=edit&redlink=1 "Leon de Beylié (page does not exist)") added to the museum's collection by donating four famous paintings by [Francisco de Zurbarán](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francisco_de_Zurbar%C3%A1n "Francisco de Zurbarán"), continuing a long tradition of donations and bequests. De Beylié had a direct and massive influence on the wealth and the nature of the collections. From 1895 until his accidental death on 15 July 1910, he bought for the museum 50 paintings, 13 drawings, 16 sculptures, 13 pieces of archeology and hundreds of objects from the Far East.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-8)

From 1920 to the early-1950s, the Museum of Grenoble was considered the premier museum of contemporary art in France, since the Paris museum did not open until 1947. It was even one of the first museums in the world, together with the [_Folkwang Museum_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_Folkwang "Museum Folkwang") in [Essen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Essen "Essen") (Germany) and the _Muzeum Sztuki_ in [Łódź](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C5%81%C3%B3d%C5%BA "Łódź") (Poland), as well as the [Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Modern_Art "Museum of Modern Art") in New York which did not open until 1929.

In 1982, President [François Mitterrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Mitterrand "François Mitterrand") announced a plan to construct a new building. The following year, the new mayor of Grenoble Alain Carignon, and the Minister of Culture [Jack Lang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jack_Lang_(French_politician) "Jack Lang (French politician)"), agreed on the idea and on the site of the new building, on a parking lot near the centre of town. After the selection of architects in 1987, construction began in 1990.

On January 30, 1994, the new building housing the collections was inaugurated by Prime Minister [Édouard Balladur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%89douard_Balladur "Édouard Balladur"). Located in the heart of the city, bordering the [Isère River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)"), it tripled the exhibition space of the old museum. Its total cost was 203 million French francs (31 million euros). To complete the Museum there is a sculpture garden in the Albert Michallon park, a wooded area of 16,000 m 2 surrounding the old city wall from the late 19th century.

## History of the location of the new museum

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History of the location of the new museum")]

The current location of the museum was occupied since the 13th century by the great monastery of the [Brothers Minor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_Friars_Minor "Order of Friars Minor"), known in France as the Cordeliers or [Franciscans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franciscans "Franciscans") until they moved to the current Berulle Square in 1592.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-9) Integrated into the city in the 13th century by an extension of the Roman wall, the place was at the eastern extremity of the town and remained so until the 19th century, while different generations of fortifications were built over the centuries.

Thus was built the Tower of the Island in 1401, serving as a defence system that allowed relative autonomy for the consuls of the city who considered it to be their main "home City". In 1591, the future [Duke of Lesdiguieres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_de_Bonne,_duc_de_Lesdigui%C3%A8res "François de Bonne, duc de Lesdiguières"), who came to take possession of the city during the religious wars, built a new fortified wall, turning the place into a small fortress called _Arsenal_ to protect himself from any rebellion of the inhabitants. In this way the area became the first barracks in the history of the city.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-10)

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3d/Mur_d%27enceinte_1888_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Mur_d%27enceinte_1888_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mur_d'enceinte_1888_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG)

The 1888 Wall in the museum

In the 19th century, General [Haxo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois_Nicolas_Beno%C3%AEt,_Baron_Haxo "François Nicolas Benoît, Baron Haxo") enlarged the precincts of the city from 1832 to 1836 by building a new fortification wall close to the _Arsenal_. Historically a place of military occupation, the area was occupied during the 19th century by several barracks of which Vinoy barracks was on the site of the museum and the Bizanet barracks was opposite. [_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

Around 1888, a change was made to the Haxo wall.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-11) At the urging of the mayor, Edouard Rey, and the population, the engineer created a new gate, the Gate of _Saulaie_ to serve the new district of [Green Island](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C3%8Ele_Verte_(Grenoble) "Île Verte (Grenoble)"). This new gate obliged the military for technical reasons to correct the path of the Haxo wall, building a new line of wall square to the old wall down to the edge of the [Isère River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Is%C3%A8re_(river) "Isère (river)") at the site of an old [Ravelin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ravelin "Ravelin") fortification. This new wall of 150 linear meters has been preserved from the sculpture garden to the football field then going through part of the structure of the Museum. In 1967 the [Vinoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Vinoy "Joseph Vinoy") barracks were demolished, leaving room for a large parking lot.

## Architecture building

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Architecture building")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Hall_d%27accueil_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG/250px-Hall_d%27accueil_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hall_d'accueil_-_Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble.JPG)

Lobby of the museum

The present building of 18,270 sq.m.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-12) was inaugurated in 1994 as part of a program of large works in the province initiated in 1982. It was designed by architects Olivier Félix-Faure, Antoine Félix-Faure and Philippe Macary from the architectural firm from Grenoble _Groupe6_, assisted by museographer Lorenzo Piqueras.

On the site there were severe design constraints. The imperatives were in respect to the immediate vicinity of the site. To the North-west a part of the Lesdiguieres wall dating from 1591 are recorded as being historical monuments. Nearby, the _Tower of the Island_ dating from 1401, is also a register structure. To the east, the modified part of the wall built around 1888 must be conserved, forcing the integration of part of it inside the building. Finally to the east, access to a football stadium must to be retained during the development of the structure for an area with high urban population density.

The museum is built over a huge parking lot on three levels keeping it safe from flooding from the Isère River.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-13) For the exhibition areas, the museum itself is built on three levels, but most of the display halls are located at level 0. At this level, the halls are served by a wide central aisle. On the left are the five sequences of ancient art, on the right are temporary exhibitions. The end of the aisle has been left empty of any work, in an arc, this huge area is dedicated to the 20th century, and also gives access to the Tower of the Island.

Levels -1 and -2 are smaller floors, and thus have a limited number of rooms. Their lighting is no longer an overhead light useful for study as in the halls of level 0. At level-1 has installed after the lobby, three rooms of Greek, Etruscan and Egyptian antiquities, and at the other end of the building, four rooms covering art at the end of the 20th century (after 1960). Below, level-2 has six rooms for the 21st century. It is also at this level that leads to the spectacular integration of the end of the 19th century wall into this futuristic building.

A few metres from the building, the museum features via a skywalk of glass and steel, the Tower of the Island, transforming it into a place of exhibition graphics. The architecture also incorporates the district football stadium into the complex.

Inside, the transitions between levels are equipped with wide ramps and three lifts to travel between floors. The rooms are designed to rest the eye: uniform wooden floors, white walls, etc.

Around the cylindrical entry hall, are the reception counter, library, shop, and cafeteria. Upstairs museum offices, as well as those of the Association of Friends of the Museum, the Association of Museum in Music, which organizes concerts in an auditorium of 275 seats in partnership with [The Louvre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Louvre "The Louvre") and finally the André Chastel library equipped with a specialized collection of 55,000 art history books available to consult on site.

## Museum curators

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Museum_of_Grenoble&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Museum curators")]

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/27/Alexandre_Debelle_by_Jacques_Gay_-_1881.jpg/250px-Alexandre_Debelle_by_Jacques_Gay_-_1881.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alexandre_Debelle_by_Jacques_Gay_-_1881.jpg)

[Alexandre Debelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Debelle "Alexandre Debelle"), curator from 1853 to 1887. Portrait by [Jacques Gay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Gay "Jacques Gay")

Two Curators have made a special mark on the history of the museum: Louis-Joseph Jay and Andry-Farcy. The first created and ensured the implementation of the museum from 1798 to 1815,[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-14) before leaving the estate to Benjamin Rolland. Painters [Alexandre Debelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandre_Debelle "Alexandre Debelle") and Jules Bernard ensured the succession as preservationists.

Then during the 20th century, there were Xavier Borgey and in particular Pierre André Farcy, called Andry-Farcy, curator from 1919 to 1949, who decisively guided the museum in favour of the collection of modern art. He left but agreed to come back in exchange for the promise of displaying a number of contemporary works by Matisse, Picasso and Monnet beside some of the great works of the museum. This caused a violent press campaign against him. His opponents would come to name his art gallery, the "rigolarium" [comedy house]. His successors were Jean Leymarie, Gabrielle Kueny, Maurice Besset, [Marie-Claude Beaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Claude_Beaud "Marie-Claude Beaud"), [Pierre Gaudibert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Gaudibert "Pierre Gaudibert"), Hélène Vincent (Temporary for 2 years), Serge Lemoine, [Guy Tosatto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guy_Tosatto "Guy Tosatto"), and since 2024 Sebastien Gokalp[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mus%C3%A9e_de_Grenoble#cite_note-15).
